Draft:

I agree with the principal's decision that every student should take part in at least one extracurricular activity. Some students may groan at first, but clubs, teams, and other groups teach things that a classroom cannot. They build friendships, they teach responsibility, and they help students find out what they are good at.

First, activities bring students together who might never meet otherwise. In a big school, it is easy to spend all day with the same small group of friends. When a quiet student joins the robotics club or the school play, he works side by side with people from different grades and backgrounds. My cousin was shy in ninth grade until she joined the cross-country team. Running long miles with teammates gave her something to talk about, and by the end of the season she had a whole new circle of friends. A rule that pushes students to join something gives everyone that chance, not just the outgoing kids.

Second, extracurricular activities teach responsibility in a way that homework alone does not. A yearbook staff member has to meet deadlines, or the whole book is late. A soccer player who skips practice lets down the team, not just himself. These students learn to manage their time, show up when others are counting on them, and keep promises. Those are the same habits employers and colleges look for, and it is better to practice them now, when the stakes are small.

Third, activities help students discover interests and talents. Many people never know they enjoy debate, painting, or coding until they try it. A student who is struggling in math might find that she is a natural leader on the student council, and that confidence can carry back into her classes. Without a requirement, many students would never take that first step.

Some people argue that students are already too busy with jobs or family duties. That is a fair concern, but the rule only asks for one activity, and schools can offer options that meet once a week or during lunch. A small commitment is reasonable for such large benefits.

For these reasons, I support the principal's decision. Requiring one activity helps students connect, grow, and find out who they can become.
